I don't think that this is much of a surprise.

Office really doesn't have any compelling reason to be sold as a service. It just doesn't; the functions it has done have been carried out on local machines for decades, and they have been done very well. External support for this type of function only introduces new vulnerabilities, as has been demonstrated during outages (better hope you don't have a term paper due the next day). It also subjects you to the risks of having all your files on the Internet, with one of those risks being a data-hungry corporation having control of them.

Plus, you have to pay on a continuous basis for the 'privilege,' and on top of that the bulk of the software sits on your machine, taking up hard drive space, yet useless without an ongoing subscription, ensuring that your computer's resources will be used for the bulk of the storage and processing. On the other hand, you can have Office licensed in perpetuity to you personally. Although newer licenses were intended to only ever be installed on one computer and never transferred, assuming that you actually listened to the stupid thing, you could just get an earlier version where you could move it between computers; by this point Office is a pretty mature product and you can safely hang back on a much older version and not miss out on much, and avoid the pitfalls of having Office run as software-as-a-service.

So yeah. Microsoft's attempt to force people to pay rent and hand even more of their personal data to their services is not all that successful. Imagine that.
